name: The Beech Arbour of Van Heekpark
age_estimate: about a century old (sources disagree on the exact planting year)
transport: About 1.8 km west of Enschede Centraal station, roughly 20-25 minutes on foot; the park borders Hengelosestraat. No specific bus stop verified this pass.
story:
The beech arbour of Van Heekpark contains no beech.

Its Dutch name, Beukenberceau, translates straight across to beech arbour, and the tree actually doing the work is haagbeuk: hornbeam, Carpinus betulus, a different family altogether. Hornbeam gets the job on temperament. It takes hard clipping year after year and holds an architectural shape for decades, which is why gardeners across Europe reach for it whenever a tunnel has to stay a tunnel.

Roughly a hundred of them stand here in two trained rows, pruned into a green corridor that serves as the main link between G.J. van Heekpark and the Van Lochemsbleekpark beside it.

When it went in is genuinely unsettled. The national register of monumental trees says the park was laid out in 1917 and 1918 and that the berceau was made then. The Rijksmonument description says the berceau was built in 1929, at the south-eastern end of the Van Lochemsbleekpark woods. Nothing establishes whether those are one job described twice or a planting later extended, so both dates stay on the page.

The park came out of the textile boom. Garden architect P.H. Wattez designed it for Gerrit Jan van Heek, one of the mill owners whose factories made the modern city, and van Heek handed it to the municipality in 1918. The mills are long closed. The tunnel is still clipped, and both parks have been a single national monument since 1995.

This is one to walk through rather than stand in front of.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the clipped green tunnel of about a hundred hornbeams, trained in two rows and arched overhead, whatever the beech in its Dutch name suggests. It runs between G.J. van Heekpark and the Van Lochemsbleekpark.

name: The Plane Tree of Klokkenplas
transport: In the city centre, roughly 1-1.5 km / a 15-20 minute walk from Enschede Centraal station.
story:
The garden this tree belonged to is gone. The tree is still standing in the middle of where it was.

The national register of monumental trees records the plane on the Klokkenplas as a remnant of a garden of the van Heek family, and dates its planting to somewhere between 1860 and 1870. A 2026 survey of the city's historic planes by the local heritage foundation puts the group it belongs to at 140 to 160 years, a little younger and clearly overlapping. Around a century and a half is as tight as the two sources honestly get.

That is long enough to have stood through the plot around it turning from private ground into a public square, and through Enschede becoming a textile city and then ceasing to be one.

It has company. The same survey counts it among a small set of monumental planes in the centre, alongside the Bomen van Herman on the Noorderhagen and the plane on the Cort van der Lindelaan, which is itself what remains of a country garden the city built over in the 1920s. Three trees, three vanished gardens, an easy walk between them.

The heritage foundation called its piece on these planes "if trees could talk". This one would spend most of the conversation on things that are no longer here.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the plane's camouflage bark, flaking in cream, olive and grey, and by the bristly seed balls that hang on into winter. It stands on the Klokkenplas square in the city centre.
